newsitem.title: GERMANY: Suspected RAF guerrilla expects life jail sentence.
newsitem.headline: Suspected RAF guerrilla expects life jail sentence.

text.p: An urban guerrilla charged with killing two U.S. soldiers and attempting to murder Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Tuesday she expected to receive a life jail sentence.

Birgit Hogefeld, a member of the RAF group which waged a sporadic war of killing and kidnapping against the establishment, said the judges had made up their minds before her trial began in November 1994.

"I do not think that anyone who watched this trial would have any doubt that I will be sentenced to life in prison," Hogefeld told journalists before reading a 31-page statement to the court in closing her defence.
"The evidence does not support the life prison term but for RAF members that has been the norm and that will be the case here," she said, adding that she now had "a vast inner distance" from the RAF.

Hogefeld is charged with involvement in the 1985 bombing of a United States air base in Frankfurt in which a soldier and a civilian were killed. Another soldier was killed before the bombing so that his identity card could be used.
She is also accused of taking part in a 1988 attempt to kill Tietmeyer, who was then Finance Ministry state secretary and is now president of the German central bank.
Tietmeyer testified at her trial that he had stared down the barrel of an assassin's gun which fired off two to four shots before his car escaped.
The five judges are expected to issue their verdict next Tuesday, ending what considered to be the last major trial in Germany involving the RAF.

Hogefeld said the judges has already decided she was guilty because of the controversy over her arrest in June 1993 when police ambushed her and companion Wolfgang Grams at a railway station in the northern town of Bad Kleinen.

Grams shot policeman Michael Newrzella and then himself in a chaotic shootout after Hogefeld had already been seized. Activists claimed police shot Grams in cold blood but independent inquiries found that he shot himself in the head.
Prosecutors have charged Hogefeld with Newrzella's murder, arguing that she was jointly responsible because she and Grams both carried guns and had agreed to use them to resist arrest.
"I have been charged with the murder of a man even though I was pinned to the ground with a police gun pointed at my head before even the first shot was fired," she said.
